title: PDF export
description: PDF export renders documents to fixed pages: HTML->PDF (headless browser), programmatic (ReportLab), or typeset (LaTeX). The challenges are pagination (no widowed headings), fonts (embedded subsets), and fidelity (what you see = the PDF). Server-side rendering keeps it consistent; the export is deterministic for the same input.
mechanism: Render pipeline: content -> layout (paged) -> PDF. Headless Chromium for HTML fidelity; ReportLab for programmatic; LaTeX for typeset quality. Fonts embedded.

title: CSV/JSON export
description: CSV/JSON export is the data interchange workhorse: flatten nested structures (JSON paths as columns), handle types (dates as ISO, nulls as empty), stream large results, and quote correctly (CSV injection: cells starting with = are a security issue — prefix with '). The export respects the current filters — what you see is what exports.
mechanism: Flatten nested -> typed columns -> stream rows -> quote (CSV) / encode (JSON). CSV injection guard. Filters applied first.
algo: O(rows) streaming; injection guard O(1) per cell.
demo:
import csv, io

rows = [{'name': 'a', 'tags': ['x', 'y'], 'n': 1}, {'name': '=cmd', 'tags': [], 'n': 2}]

def safe(cell):  # CSV injection guard
    s = str(cell)
    return "'" + s if s[:1] in ('=', '+', '-', '@') else s

buf = io.StringIO()
w = csv.writer(buf)
w.writerow(['name', 'tags', 'n'])
for r in rows:
    w.writerow([safe(r['name']), safe(','.join(r['tags'])), r['n']])
print(buf.getvalue(), end='')
print('flattened nested; injection-guarded (=cmd); streams for large')

title: Streaming export
description: Streaming export never holds the dataset in memory: rows flow from the query through the formatter to the download, chunk by chunk. The HTTP response streams (chunked encoding); the user sees progress immediately. Backpressure propagates — if the client is slow, the query slows. Million-row exports are routine this way; buffered exports OOM.
mechanism: Generator pipeline: query cursor -> format row -> yield chunk. Chunked HTTP. Backpressure via the generator (slow consumer slows producer).
algo: O(rows) time, O(1) memory. The only sane way at scale.

title: Export pagination
description: Paginated export handles data larger than one file: split by row count (10k rows/file), by time (one file/day), or by key range. The manifest lists the parts; consumers reassemble. Pagination composes with streaming (each part streams). The part naming is deterministic (part-0001.csv) for automation.
mechanism: Partition strategy (count/time/key) -> numbered parts -> manifest. Deterministic naming. Each part independently valid (headers repeated).
algo: O(rows) total; parts O(1) each to consume.
demo:
# paginate by row count: each part independently valid
rows = [{'id': i} for i in range(2500)]
PAGE = 1000
parts = [rows[i:i+PAGE] for i in range(0, len(rows), PAGE)]
manifest = []
for n, part in enumerate(parts):
    name = 'part-%04d.csv' % (n + 1)
    manifest.append({'file': name, 'rows': len(part), 'header': True})
print('parts:', [(m['file'], m['rows']) for m in manifest])
print('manifest.json lists parts; headers repeated per part; deterministic names')

title: Large dataset export
description: Large exports need the full toolkit: streaming (O(1) memory), pagination (manageable parts), compression (gzip on the fly), checksums per part (verify), and resume (checkpoint per part). The export runs as a background job (this lane's task center) with progress. A 100GB export is routine with this machinery — and impossible without it.
mechanism: Background job: stream -> compress -> part files -> checksums -> manifest -> notify. Resume from the manifest. Progress = parts done / total.

title: Scheduled exports
description: Scheduled exports run unattended: cron triggers the pipeline, results land in storage/email, failures alert. The schedule is declarative (every Monday 9am), the run is idempotent (same period = same output, safe to retry), and retention prunes old exports. Timezones are explicit — '9am' means a named zone.
mechanism: Scheduler (cron) -> idempotent job -> deliver (storage/email) -> alert on failure -> retention prune. Timezone explicit in the schedule.
demo:
# idempotent scheduled export: same period -> same output (safe retry)
store = {}

def run_export(period):  # period = '2026-W43'
    if period in store:
        return 'skipped (already exported: idempotent)'
    store[period] = 'report-%s.pdf' % period
    return 'exported ' + store[period]

print(run_export('2026-W43'))
print(run_export('2026-W43'), '(retry safe)')
print('cron: 0 9 * * MON America/New_York (timezone EXPLICIT)')

title: Export APIs
description: Export APIs let programs pull data: REST endpoints with format params (?format=csv), async jobs for large exports (POST -> job id -> poll -> download URL), and webhooks on completion. Auth and rate limits apply; the API returns the same bytes as the UI export (one pipeline, two doors). Pagination and cursors for programmatic consumers.
mechanism: Sync for small (?format=), async job for large (202 + poll), webhook on done. One pipeline behind UI + API. Signed download URLs.

title: Export validation
description: Export validation checks the output before delivery: schema conformance (columns, types), row counts (match the source query), checksums (per part), and spot-checks (sample rows match source). Invalid exports never deliver — the job fails loudly. Validation is part of the pipeline, not an afterthought.
mechanism: Post-export checks: schema, counts, checksums, samples. Fail = alert + no delivery. The manifest records validation results.
demo:
# validate before delivery: schema, counts, checksums, samples
source_count = 1000
exported = [{'id': i, 'v': i*2} for i in range(1000)]

checks = {
    'row count': len(exported) == source_count,
    'schema': all(set(r) == {'id', 'v'} for r in exported[:10]),
    'sample': exported[42] == {'id': 42, 'v': 84},
}
for name, ok in checks.items():
    print('%-10s %s' % (name, 'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'))
print('all pass -> deliver; any fail -> alert, NO delivery')

title: Export error handling
description: Export errors are handled, not hoped away: query failures retry with backoff, disk-full pauses (not corrupts), partial parts are deleted (never delivered half), and the job records the failure with context. The user gets a clear message ('export failed: source timeout, retrying') not a corrupt file. Idempotency makes retries safe.
mechanism: Retry with backoff (transient); pause on resource exhaustion; delete partials on failure; structured error records; user-facing status. Idempotent = safe retry.

title: Export progress UX
description: Export progress UX keeps users informed: determinate progress (parts done/total), ETA, current stage ('compressing part 3/12'), and cancellation. For quick exports the progress is a brief toast; for long ones a persistent job (the task center). The progress is honest — measured, not animated.
mechanism: Progress = parts done/total (measured); stage labels; ETA from rate; cancel button (aborts cleanly). Quick: toast. Long: persistent job.
demo:
# honest progress: measured parts, ETA from rate, cancellable
import time

total, done, t0 = 12, 0, time.perf_counter()
cancelled = False
for part in range(total):
    if cancelled:
        print('cancelled: partials cleaned up')
        break
    time.sleep(0.01)
    done += 1
    rate = done / (time.perf_counter() - t0)
    eta = (total - done) / rate
    print('\rpart %2d/%d  ETA %.1fs  stage=compressing' % (done, total, eta), end='')
print('\ndone: measured progress, cancellable, honest ETA')

title: Testing exports
description: Exports are tested end-to-end: reference files (golden masters) compared byte-for-byte, round-trips (export -> import -> identical), large-scale runs (memory stays O(1)), and failure injection (kill mid-export -> clean state). The golden files live in the repo; CI regenerates and diffs. An export that can't round-trip is broken.
mechanism: Golden masters; round-trip tests; memory profiling on large runs; failure injection. CI regenerates goldens on template changes (reviewed diff).
demo:
import csv, io

# round-trip: export -> import -> identical
rows = [{'a': 1, 'b': 'x'}, {'a': 2, 'b': 'y,z'}]
buf = io.StringIO()
w = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=['a', 'b'])
w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)
buf.seek(0)
back = list(csv.DictReader(buf))
back = [{'a': int(r['a']), 'b': r['b']} for r in back]
print('round-trip identical:', back == rows)
print('golden masters: byte-compare in CI; failure injection: kill mid-export')
